extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics writers (students, researchers, textbook authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for producing clear mathematical exposition (papers, books, lectures), covering content, audience, organization, notation, style, and revision practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say something
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to say something well you must have something to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing about nothing or trying to say too many disparate things. Good works (short or long) have a clearly delineated subject; organize around a single unambiguous idea or tightly related set of ideas. Use central, crucial examples and counterexamples as the backbone of exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak to someone
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide who you want to reach (your audience) and write for that person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the audience both generally (e.g., specialists, second-year grad students) and, if helpful, as a concrete imagined reader. Tailor motivation, informality, level of detail, and repetition to that audience. Anticipate and avoid readers' likely difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize first (make an outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you know what to say and to whom, make an outline listing heuristics, lemmas, theorems, corollaries, remarks, and proofs in a logically correct and psychologically digestible order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish organization (what the main headings/subheadings are and their connections) from arrangement (linear ordering). Good organization shows where parts belong and provides visible interconnections; preparation of an outline can take a long time and may require revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange for psychological digestibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange material so the reader knows what to expect while still encountering well-placed surprises; parts should fit and become visible when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the order so lemmas appear when needed, emphasize appropriately, indicate interconnections, and avoid forcing the reader through convoluted dependencies. Tight organization aids both teaching and later reuse by readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about the alphabet (notation) early
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest time early to design consistent, helpful notation and choose letters carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad ad hoc notation introduced mid-composition usually creates headaches; plan alphabets, fonts, upper/lowercase roles, and anticipate symbols for functions, points, measures, etc. Good notation has 'alphabetical harmony' and avoids near-dissonances (e.g., conflicting uses of the same symbol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid freezing letters and unhelpful naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'freeze' symbols by committing them unnecessarily to single meanings that prevent flexible, consistent notation elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conventions that make letters unusable in other contexts (e.g., permanently making x,y,z be points) and avoid awkward uses like ad hoc acronyms or overloading subscripts/superscripts that confuse rather than clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in spirals (iterative drafting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write chapters/sections in an iterative order (1,2,1,2,3,1,2,3,4, ...) and expect to rewrite earlier parts as later material clarifies them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spiral writing and reorganization are natural: produce a first draft quickly (spilling your heart), then rewrite whole sections/chapters multiple times rather than merely editing. Rewriting means writing again—be merciless about wholesale changes and omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite, don't merely edit
rubrics_metrics.description: When revising, prefer complete rewrites to piecemeal editing with a red pencil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red-pencil edits lead to catastrophic blunders and incoherence; aim to produce a clean typescript others can work from. After several rewrites produce a polished version for readers and then a final typescript based on that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work steadily and prime the pump
rubrics_metrics.description: Write small amounts steadily every day and end each session by preparing a clear starting point for the next day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop each day by priming the pump (decide the next section/title/first sentence) to sustain creative momentum and overcome inertia. Small, regular progress accumulates into large results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize always (spiral organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continue organizing while writing; review earlier sections from the viewpoint of new material and use repeated, deeper mentions to prepare later formal treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a concept, motivate it, define it, give examples/counterexamples, then in later sections review prior material from the new viewpoint. Use 'subplots' and gradual preparation (mentioning a term early, expanding it later) to help readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build around central examples and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize work around concrete examples and counterexamples; big general thoughts often rest on small but profound special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers need guidance to see what proofs do not prove and where counterexamples lie. Avoid exhaustive formal detail when it obscures the conceptual heart; point out the appropriate counterexamples and directions to go next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sparing with labels and displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Label displays (equations, formulae, inequalities) only when there is a reason to reference them later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary labels waste reader attention; name displays when they will be used. Conversely, be careful not to under-label when a reference aids clarity. Avoid misleading or misplaced labels that force the reader to search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrelevant assumptions and the trivial but be explicit about trivial cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not drag in irrelevant hypotheses; explicitly mention and exclude trivial cases when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrelevant assumptions or emphasis confuse readers. Also, failing to address trivial cases (e.g., the zero case) can mislead; indicate trivial exceptions or promise counterexamples when needed to maintain confidence and avoid misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write proofs forward (human-readable proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs in a forward, human-intelligible order rather than the classical backward 'given s let ...' style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward proofs are more graspable and rememberable: start with what you know and proceed step-by-step toward the goal, explaining the key ideas rather than just showing a chain of equalities the reader must decode. Use typical small cases to illustrate general proofs when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols and punctuation correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent and unambiguous in symbol usage; punctuate symbolic sentences as you would verbal ones and avoid starting sentences with symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a symbol's verbal reading is consistent (e.g., read '∈' as 'is in'). Punctuate equations/inequalities and don't overwork periods/commas; where a sentence would be clearer with words, prefer them (e.g., 'For invertible X, the adjoint X* ...'). Layout and page appearance also influence readability—balance prose and displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write good English (or appropriate vernacular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correct grammar, diction, punctuation, and spelling according to commonly accepted standards of the language of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good language should be unobtrusive and free the reader to focus on content. Avoid colloquial misuse and cumulative abrasions from bad diction. Keep references like Fowler, Roget, Webster handy for guidance. This applies to other languages substituting the appropriate standard references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about status of statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader the status of claims: what has been proved, what hasn't, what will be proved later, and what is standard or irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't gloss over difficulties or mislead with 'obvious' assertions; if you don't know whether something holds, confess failure or promise a later treatment. Use 'obvious' only when you genuinely have verified it (e.g., by seminar acceptance or re-checking after ripening).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'obvious' and similar phrases carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve 'obvious' and 'easy to see' for genuinely obvious facts and ensure they are true and checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether you still consider the assertion obvious after time has passed or after explaining it to others. If in doubt, provide a brief justification or indicate where the argument is standard or will be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive, irrelevant notation and repetitive mechanical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't burden the reader with frozen notation, intrusive labels, or long chains of obvious equalities; prefer readable explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical code-like presentations that are machine-verifiable but human-unfriendly should be replaced by explanatory paragraphs that describe the transformations. Use illustrative small cases instead of long enumerations when appropriate (e.g., prove 3x3 case to show general pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout, architecture, and balance of prose and displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the printed page or blackboard appearance: balance prose and symbolic displays so the reader's eye and mind are helped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pages of solid prose (sermony) or pages full of undecorated symbols (frightening). Break up text with displays, use enough prose to prevent drowning in notation, and for lectures beware of blackboard cram—let ideas grow in view.

rubrics_metrics.name: All communication is exposition (adapt your medium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Books, articles, lectures, and letters share the same exposition problems but differ in practical constraints (attention span, ability to backtrack).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan lectures differently: keep oral difficulties in mind, omit computations that a hearer can't follow, and use the blackboard to make material come alive. For papers, allow readers the ability to pause and check proofs; adapt content and omission to the medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend your style against mechanical copy-editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to defend mathematically meaningful stylistic choices against editorial assistants who mechanically apply rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/copyreaders often misapply typographical or stylistic rules (quotation punctuation, hyphenation, word order) in ways that change meaning. Authors should be ready to argue for logical/semantic punctuation and phrasing and to preserve mathematically significant typography (e.g., 'measure-preserving' vs 'nonmeasure preserving').

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to stop (be ruthless about finishing)
rubrics_metrics.description: After proofreading, checking computations, and letting the manuscript ripen, stop polishing and finish the work ruthlessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is always more to say, but at some point further polishing yields diminishing returns and endless mirages of improvement. Read the manuscript quickly from a rested point of view to test major points, then stop and send it on.
